title: How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?
gist: IEEE Spectrum details Japan's MMX mission, launched 20 October 2026 on an H3 rocket, which aims to land on Phobos, deploy the Idefix rover, and return a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. The piece covers the engineering challenges of microgravity landing, quasi-satellite orbits, dual sampling devices and international partnerships, including NASA's contribution via a Blue Origin subsidiary.

insights.claim: MMX launched on Japan's H3 rocket from Tanegashima on 20 October 2026, will reach Mars in 2027, and aims to deliver a 10-gram Phobos sample to Earth in the second half of 2031.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Fixes the schedule for a major Japanese flagship deep-space milestone and a validation point for H3.
insights.locator: More than 10 years in the making

insights.claim: MMX has three modules: a propulsion module for cruise and Mars orbit insertion, an exploration module with the rover and sampling gear, and a return module carrying the capsule.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Modular staging and jettisoning drive mass and risk allocation; sample return depends on every stage working.
insights.locator: MMX consists of three modules

insights.claim: If the Mars orbit insertion burn fails, MMX will fly past Mars and be flung into the solar system, making the capture burn a single-point failure.
insights.speaker: Nicola Baresi
insights.so_what: Mission success hinges on one extended, carefully timed burn with no fallback.
insights.quote: “If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,”
insights.locator: How MMX Will Orbit Phobos

insights.claim: Mission planners called MMX the most complex mission its co-principal investigator has seen, with orbits around Phobos complicated by periodic Mars-caused communications blackouts with Earth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Michel
insights.so_what: Complexity raises schedule and failure risk versus Hayabusa-class missions.
insights.quote: “It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,”
insights.locator: More than 10 years in the making

insights.claim: MMX will use a quasi-satellite orbit because Phobos is too small to orbit conventionally, flying an egg-shaped path alongside the moon, and will retreat to a larger stable orbit during the roughly two-week blackout when Mars passes behind the Sun.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Illustrates orbital design innovation needed for small-body missions.
insights.locator: Since Phobos is too small to orbit

insights.claim: Existing best images of Phobos have only a few meters per pixel resolution, so MMX's two-year remote sensing campaign with cameras and a laser altimeter at 200 km to under 20 km distance is needed to pick landing sites.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Landing site selection is data-limited until MMX maps the surface at higher resolution.
insights.locator: The best existing images of Phobos

insights.claim: The 23-kilogram Idefix rover, built by CNES and DLR with JAXA, will be released in 2028 or early 2029 from 40 to 100 meters altitude as a scout, a "first penguin", before the main lander attempts touchdown.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Sequencing the rover first de-risks the main landing and shows how international partners share risk.
insights.locator: Idefix Rover: The First Penguin

insights.claim: The rover drop recalls the 2005 Hayabusa MINERVA failure, where release at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters caused the rover to miss Itokawa and drift into deep space.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Release altitude error is a known failure mode in low-gravity deployment.
insights.locator: It will be a tense moment

insights.claim: Idefix will land unprotected at under 1 meter per second, will probably bounce several times, then use four legs to right itself autonomously and unfold solar panels.
insights.speaker: Stephan Ulamec
insights.so_what: The landing outcome is acknowledged to be hard to predict; self-righting is the key design hedge.
insights.locator: Idefix will get a slight nudge

insights.claim: Idefix will move at most one millimeter per second on paddle-like bladed wheels because faster driving in microgravity would be more like swimming than driving.
insights.speaker: Cecily Sunday
insights.so_what: Mobility in microgravity is limited to crawl speeds, constraining science return per day.
insights.quote: “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,”
insights.locator: Once operational, Idefix will roll

insights.claim: Earth-based tests on regolith simulants can approximate Phobos rover motion fairly well if the rover moves very slowly with the same materials and weight, per the Idefix WheelCam researcher.
insights.speaker: Cecily Sunday
insights.so_what: Supports ground testing as a cost-effective proxy for low-gravity surface operations.
insights.locator: Despite the microgravity

insights.claim: Idefix's 100-Earth-day primary mission will yield sub-millimeter-resolution data on porosity, grain size and surface strength, filling the gap between orbital observations and returned samples.
insights.speaker: Stephan Ulamec
insights.so_what: Ground truth from the rover informs where and how the main spacecraft lands.
insights.locator: Idefix’s interactions with its new home

insights.claim: OSIRIS-REx's arm sank nearly half a meter into Bennu's loose material, but the Idefix co-PI does not expect Idefix to sink deep into Phobos because Bennu is much smaller at 500 meters in diameter.
insights.speaker: Stephan Ulamec
insights.so_what: Regolith behavior on rubble-pile bodies remains a real uncertainty for landing design.
insights.locator: When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft

insights.claim: The main lander will descend to about 10 meters and free-fall the rest, and with so little gravity even small sideways motion could tip it or make it bounce away; Kawakatsu compares it to landing a balloon.
insights.speaker: Yasuhiro Kawakatsu
insights.so_what: Touchdown stability is the central engineering risk and the gate to the sample payoff.
insights.quote: “I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,”
insights.locator: How MMX Will Land and Collect Samples

insights.claim: Surface operations are limited to roughly two hours on Phobos for sampling before liftoff.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: The brief window forces highly automated sampling with little room for error.
insights.locator: A successful, upright landing

insights.claim: MMX carries two samplers for redundancy: a JAXA coring sampler reaching at least 2 centimeters deep and a NASA pneumatic sampler made by Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, that injects nitrogen gas to stir up grains.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Shows commercial-space supplier participation in a Japanese flagship mission and a hedge against hard terrain.
insights.locator: MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices

insights.claim: If Phobos's surface is very hard the coring sampler may struggle, but the pneumatic sampler would not have that problem, which is why the dual system adds redundancy.
insights.speaker: Yasuhiro Kawakatsu
insights.so_what: Redundant tooling is the designed hedge against unknown surface properties.
insights.locator: The dual system also adds redundancy

insights.claim: JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams from below the weathered surface, which has been battered by solar radiation, cosmic rays and micrometeorites, because deeper material should better record Phobos's origins.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Subsurface sampling raises scientific value but needs a robotic arm that has never been used this way.
insights.locator: Probing beneath the top layer

insights.claim: Phobos's origin is unknown, with two leading theories: captured asteroids from the belt, or debris from a giant impact on Mars; MMX data aims to discriminate between them.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Resolving origin would shape models of how terrestrial planets form.
insights.locator: Why Phobos Is Such a Strange Moon

insights.claim: Phobos is a lumpy rubble pile about 27 kilometers long with 1/1,800th of Earth's gravity, so an adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Extremely low gravity defines every landing and mobility constraint.
insights.locator: Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile

insights.claim: Phobos has likely been peppered by Martian ejecta, so the sample may contain a few hundred Mars grains identifiable by oxygen isotopes, potentially the first Martian samples returned to Earth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Michel
insights.so_what: A cheaper route to Martian material than a dedicated Mars sample-return mission.
insights.quote: “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.”
insights.locator: One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX

insights.claim: An expert panel concluded microbes blasted off Mars would not survive ejection and radiation, so MMX avoids the expensive quarantine and containment protocols of a direct Mars sample return.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Planetary-protection exemption lowers mission cost and complexity versus Mars sample return.
insights.locator: That possibility raises a planetary-protection question

insights.claim: The 60-centimeter capsule will reenter at roughly 12 kilometers per second and land in Australia, with samples curated by JAXA's Institute of Space and Astronautical Science and shared with partners; the return leg begins in November 2030.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Reentry survival and a 2030 departure window are the final schedule gates.
insights.locator: Finally, in 2031

insights.claim: Combining orbital macroscale data, rover microscale data and sample analysis lets scientists link three scales of Phobos measurement, a structure the team says makes MMX uniquely valuable.
insights.speaker: Patrick Michel
insights.so_what: Multi-scale validation raises the scientific credibility of the returned results.
insights.quote: “We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,”
insights.locator: Michel

insights.claim: Kawakatsu argues Mars sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, and that the terrestrial region likely formed dry with water and organics scattered inwards from the icy outer solar system.
insights.speaker: Yasuhiro Kawakatsu
insights.so_what: Frames MMX as a test of how habitable environments develop on rocky planets.
insights.quote: “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.”
insights.locator: Kawakatsu
